name: The Bail Project (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: people bailed out or supported pretrial at The Bail Project's US sites, and their families.
summary: The Bail Project pays bail for people in US jails who can't afford it, through a revolving fund to which about nine in ten bail dollars return, and supports them until their cases close; its bail line cost $9.0 million with overhead in the year to June 2024, for about 3,300 bailouts and 600 people in community-release pilots. Each bailout is counted as the charity's own 40 days of pretrial detention avoided, 60% of them days really saved, plus fewer convictions and sentences, better employment later, homes kept and county jail costs, valued with the site's shared figures for time in jail; most of the value is the deaths that time in jail causes, taken from a study of prison terms at half the rate for weeks in jail. The result is about 0.017 years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars, a quarter of the median of the site's global-health models: a few weeks out of jail for about $2,700 a bailout, valued on a scale where help for the world's poorest goes much further. The biggest uncertainties are how many deaths a few weeks in jail cause, how much of the counted detention clients would have served anyway, and the year's bailouts, which the charity doesn't publish; the whole model is discounted for missing data, and a gift waits about three years behind the charity's reserves.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: The Bail Project, bail assistance and client support

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

source.note: The report's figures match the audited Form 990 for the same year (total expenses $14,464,653 here against $14,332,906 on the 990, the difference the loss on uncollectible receivables the 990 reconciles; the 990 reports one programme of $10,359,791).

rows.explainer: The bail line of the year's four programme lines: paying bail through the national revolving fund, the Bail Disruptors who meet clients in jail and court, reminders, rides, referrals and the community-release pilots in Chicago, Washtenaw County and St. Louis, and grants of about $0.7 million to partner bail funds that do the same. The other three lines (policy advocacy, public education, research) are charityevals' separate advocacy model. Fiscal 2024 is the latest year with both audited spending and reach: the 2025 report gives no programme split and its cumulative counts don't move consistently (below).

rows.explainer: The service is to one person, so households here only carry the count: households_reached is clients over this size and people_reached multiplies it back. Effects on clients' families are a side effect below.

rows.explainer: Clients over household size, so that people_reached is the year's clients.

rows.label: Clients served, fiscal 2024
rows.explainer: The year's clients: bailouts and pilot clients.

rows.label: Cost per client
rows.explainer: About $2,300 a client; the cost per bailout, if the pilots are a fifth of the cost, is about $2,200.

rows.label: Days of pretrial incarceration prevented since 2018, to June 2025
rows.explainer: The charity's own estimate (2025 report); it doesn't publish the method. The same report counts 34,572 bailouts, so both are cumulative to June 2025 and their ratio is days per bailout.

rows.label: Bailouts since 2018, to June 2025
rows.explainer: Cumulative bailouts in the same report as the days prevented (the two facts are drawn together).

rows.label: Days of pretrial detention avoided per bailout (the charity's estimate)
rows.explainer: 40 days. Cross-checks: the 2024 report's cumulative 1,412,994 days over about 31,000 bailouts is 46; the fiscal-2024 change in days over its bailouts about 69. Clients' cases take a median six months to close, so the figure isn't the whole time to disposition: we read it as the time clients would have stayed in jail before getting out some other way, and ask in counterfactual_adj how much of it they really would have.

rows.label: Days of post-conviction jail or prison avoided per bailout, through better case outcomes
rows.explainer: The shared figure for a defendant released rather than detained: detained defendants plead guilty to get out and are jailed more and longer (Heaton et al. 2017; Dobbie et al. 2016): 12 days (0 to 45); the charity's 31% dismissal rate is part of what it counts. The sentences come after the case closes, a median six months.

rows.label: Median time for a client's case to close (months)

source.title: The Bail Project, Annual Report 2024 (fiscal year July 2023 to June 2024)
source.page: pp. 12-13 (PDF page 8), The clients we serve
source.quote: The median amount of time for our clients' cases to be resolved.
source.note: The figure on the page is '6 MONTHS TO RESOLVE THE CASE'.

rows.explainer: The wait before a sentence avoided would have begun, discounted.

rows.label: Years of incarceration avoided per bailout, discounted
rows.explainer: Pretrial days now plus sentence days after the case closes, discounted at the shared rate: about 0.14 years.

rows.label: Fall in missed court dates from reminders (share of defendants)

source.title: Science News on Fishbane, Ouss and Shah (2020), Behavioral nudges reduce failure to appear for court, Science 370
source.quote: almost 38 percent of individuals in the control group missed their court dates, compared with just below 30 percent of those receiving text messages

rows.explainer: In New York City's randomised trial, text reminders cut missed dates by about 8 points for people summoned for low-level offences. The pilots add rides and referrals, but their clients are released by the courts anyway, so the reminders are the part that keeps them out of jail: 8 points (3 to 12).

rows.label: Days in jail after a missed court date (warrant, arrest, hold)
rows.explainer: A missed date brings a bench warrant; many are arrested on it and held a few days before being seen. Our judgment: 5 days (1 to 20), anchored on the short holds after warrant arrests in the Fishbane trial's setting (the trial counts the warrants avoided, about 31,000 over three years).

rows.label: Years of incarceration avoided per pilot client
rows.explainer: Missed dates avoided times the days each brings: under half a day.

rows.label: Years of incarceration avoided per client (weighted)
rows.explainer: Bailouts' and pilot clients' years, averaged over the clients; years inside a single year, so not discounted again.

rows.label: Life satisfaction lost per year in jail or prison (points)
rows.explainer: The site's shared figure for a year in prison or jail against a year outside (1.2 points, 0.5 to 3), read by every model that counts incarceration avoided. Pretrial jails are often harsher than prisons (crowding, no programmes, the shock of arrest), which the range covers.

rows.label: Share of bailed-out clients who would have lost their housing in detention
rows.explainer: Among New Yorkers held pretrial, 18% reported lost jobs and 18% lost property, the share rising with days held (Sandra Susan Smith, Federal Probation 86(3), 2022, from the New York City Criminal Justice Agency's survey); 7% of the charity's clients reported no stable housing at release (2023 report). Our judgment: 5% of clients held for weeks would lose a home (1% to 12%). Jobs lost are in the income effect below, so this counts only the home.

rows.label: Life satisfaction lost while rehousing after losing a home (points, for the time below)
rows.explainer: People without a home report life satisfaction a point or two below the housed in most surveys; a home lost after weeks in jail is usually regained within months. Our judgment: 1 point (0.4 to 2), the same order as the shared figure for incarceration.

rows.label: Time to rehouse (years)
rows.explainer: Our judgment: six months (three months to a year), most clients going to family or friends first.

rows.label: WELLBYs per client, discounted
rows.formula: ls_gain_per_person_year * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, ls_effect_years) + bailouts_fy2024 / people_reached * housing_loss_share * housing_loss_ls * housing_loss_years
rows.explainer: Incarceration's life satisfaction over the years avoided, plus the home kept by bailed-out clients.

rows.label: Formal earnings gained per released defendant a year, three to four years later (US$)
rows.explainer: The site's shared figure from Dobbie, Goldin and Yang's judge-assignment study (Philadelphia and Miami): $500 a year (0 to 2,000), mostly from fewer convictions; jobs lost in detention are in it.

rows.label: Earnings gained per client a year (US$)
rows.explainer: Bailed-out clients' gain spread over all clients; pilot clients are released anyway and gain nothing here.

rows.label: US household spending per person (Consumer Expenditure Survey, 2024)
rows.explainer: The site's one US survey consumption figure.

rows.label: Clients' consumption per person as a share of the US mean
rows.explainer: People who can't pay a $3,000 bail are poor: the poorest fifth's spending share, per household, turned into per person with the shared household sizes, as the site's other models of incarcerated people do.

rows.label: Clients' consumption per person (US$ a year)
rows.explainer: The base the earnings gain is measured against on the site's log scale.

rows.label: How long released defendants' better employment holds (years)
rows.explainer: The shared figure: measured three to four years on, 4 years (2 to 10).

rows.label: Gain in ln(consumption) per client, discounted
rows.explainer: The yearly gain on the site's log scale over the years it lasts, discounted.

rows.label: Jail costs a county saves per day a person isn't held (US$)
rows.explainer: The shared marginal cost of a jail day, $35 (15 to 80), below the $77 average the charity's own savings figure implies.

rows.label: Share of bail returned to the fund when cases close

source.title: The Bail Project, Annual Report 2024 (fiscal year July 2023 to June 2024)
source.note: 89% in the 2025 report, 91% in 2023 and 93% of closed cases in the 2024 report's fund page.

rows.explainer: The rest is forfeited for missed dates or kept by courts for fines and fees: money from donors to counties.

rows.label: Public money saved or received per client (US$)
rows.formula: (bailouts_fy2024 * days_per_bailout + pilot_clients_fy2024 * pilot_detention_years * 365) * jail_cost_per_day / people_reached + bailouts_fy2024 / people_reached * average_bail * (1 - bail_revolved_share)
rows.explainer: Jail days not paid for, and the bail that isn't returned, which counties keep.

rows.label: Value of the public money per client (units of value)
rows.explainer: Counties' money is worth what it spares their taxpayers: on the site's log scale, a dollar over consumption per person (the national-accounts mean, the site's rule for everyone's consumption), times the shared cost of public funds over how state and local taxes fall, as the site's other US models count public money.

rows.label: Deaths per year of pretrial jail, as a share of the shared prison figure
rows.explainer: The shared judgment: a few weeks in jail cause half the deaths per year that years in prison do (0.1 to 1.2), the prison figure's excess risk being highest on release.

rows.label: Deaths averted per client
rows.explainer: Years incarcerated avoided times the shared years of life lost per year, as a share of the remaining life of a person inside (40 years), at jail's share of it, discounted for the years until the deaths come (the shared figure).

rows.label: Share of deaths averted under five

source.title: The Bail Project, Annual Report 2024 (fiscal year July 2023 to June 2024)

rows.explainer: Clients are adults charged with crimes.

rows.label: Share aged 5-14 of deaths over five

source.title: The Bail Project, Annual Report 2024 (fiscal year July 2023 to June 2024)

rows.explainer: No clients under 18.

rows.label: Share aged 15-49 of deaths over fifteen

source.title: The Bail Project, Annual Report 2024 (fiscal year July 2023 to June 2024)

rows.explainer: Clients' ages; deaths come a few years later and fall a little more on older clients, so 84% (78% to 90%).

rows.label: Value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's moral weights by the age band of each death, times your value of a life: the site's one value of a death.

rows.label: Healthy years from illness averted per client
rows.explainer: Illness in jail and after (infections, untreated conditions, mental health) is in the shared life-satisfaction and mortality figures; nothing is counted twice here.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity), a multiplier
rows.explainer: The case-outcome and earnings effects are quasi-experiments on marginal defendants in Philadelphia, Miami and Harris County, a few years old; the charity's clients are people a judge set bail for that they couldn't pay, many like the marginal defendants. The days per bailout are the charity's own unpublished estimate. 0.75 (0.5 to 0.95), as the site's other models of US justice programmes (Prison Policy Initiative's decarceration branch, 0.75).

rows.label: Share of the detention clients would really have served without the charity
rows.explainer: Some clients would have got out within days by family, a bondsman, another bail fund or a judge's review, or by pleading guilty: the shared judgment for The Bail Project, 60% of the days it counts (35% to 85%). The same share applies to pilot clients, whom courts and public defenders also remind.

rows.label: The charity's share of the resources behind the release
rows.explainer: The bail and support are the charity's (with $0.7 million of grants to partner bail funds, in its cost); partner sites' own staff and donated services ($97,309 in fiscal 2025) are the rest. Public defenders' work is the case, not the release.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Share of bailed-out clients who stay out until the case closes
rows.explainer: Clients made 93% of their court dates (2024 report; 92% in 2025); some who miss one are rearrested and held again, losing part of the days counted. 0.93 (0.85 to 1).

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: Other bail funds and families pay some bail the charity would otherwise pay, and the reverse; no government pays bail. 0.95 (0.85 to 1.05), as the site's other US service models.

rows.label: Years until a donation is spent
rows.explainer: At June 2024 the charity held $50.5 million in cash, savings and investments (Form 990 for fiscal 2025, beginning-of-year balance sheet) beside $14.4 million of bail out in the courts, against spending of $14.5 million a year, and it is spending down: a $9.4 million deficit in fiscal 2025, 'intentionally operated at a budgeted deficit'. A gift now is spent when reserves run low: our judgment, 3 years (1 to 5).

rows.label: Discount for the wait until a gift is spent
rows.explainer: The shared discount rate over the wait above.

rows.label: Missing outcome data
rows.explainer: Thin: the year's bailouts are judged (bail paid over the average bail) and the effect comes from studies of release by lenient judges, not of the charity's clients; the charity's own outcome data (court return, dismissals) aren't against a comparison group. So the site's discount for missing data applies.

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.formula: evidence_adj * counterfactual_adj * attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount * missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Side effect: children and partners spared a parent's detention, as a share of the value
rows.explainer: Most clients are parents or carers; a parent jailed for weeks costs children care and income. Prison Policy Initiative's model counts 15% for longer prison terms (Wakefield and Wildeman 2013); for weeks in jail 10% (0 to 30%).

rows.label: Side effect: crime by clients while released, net of crime later avoided, as a share of the value
rows.explainer: Released defendants are 7.6 points more likely to be rearrested before their case closes, but 'no detectable effects' on crime up to four years later (Dobbie et al. 2016); in Harris County detention raises later crime (Heaton et al. 2017). The harm to victims of crimes while released is a cost: -2% of the value (-15% to +10%).

rows.label: Side effects, as a share of the value
rows.explainer: The two side effects above, each read through the side-effect weight.
